name: Pointillism
basis: why: pure dots side by side mixed by the eye; how: random dots of picture colour, complementary flecks, ground showing
note: Filed by technique (dot painting), not by Seurat's medium (oil).

lumenary.blurb: Seurat-style: the picture broken into thousands of small dots of pure colour that your eye mixes back together.

facts.bestOn: Sunlit landscapes and scenes with soft colour

why: Seurat’s idea was to stop mixing paint on a palette and put pure dots of colour side by side, leaving your eye to mix them. Seen from a distance, blue and yellow dots give a vibrating green that is brighter than mixed paint. This treatment throws thousands of dots of the picture’s own colours onto a plain ground and lets the mixing happen in the viewer.
how: Blur the picture to about the scale of one dot.
Throw dots at random positions and sizes, enough that a pixel lies under two to six of them on average.
Give each dot the colour of the blurred picture under its centre, lifted in saturation.
Wander each dot a little in hue, saturation and lightness, with up to 7 percent taking a complementary hue for the flecks that make shadows vibrate.
Let some of the plain ground show through where dots happen not to overlap.
history: Georges Seurat painted A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte in 1884 to 1886, and Paul Signac helped develop the method, called divisionism or pointillism. They drew on nineteenth century colour theory, including Michel Eugène Chevreul’s work on simultaneous contrast. The principle returns every time an image is made of dots, from halftone printing to a screen’s pixels.
uses: Fine art style portraits and landscapes
Posters and prints with a vibrating colour
terms: Colour mixed in the eye from small separate patches, not in the paint.
The colour opposite another on the colour wheel.
The practice of dividing a painting into separate patches of pure colour.
paragraphs: Seurat’s idea was not to mix paint on the palette but to put pure dots side by side and let the viewer’s eye mix them (optical mixture). The program blurs the picture to the scale of one dot, then throws dots of random position and size onto a plain ground. The number of dots is set so that, on average, a given pixel lies under 2 to 6 of them (the coverage slider). The radius is 1.5 to 7 px, and each dot varies from 0.72 to 1.22 times that.

Every dot takes the colour of the blurred picture under its centre and then wanders a little in hue, saturation and lightness (HSL), by an amount set by the colour jitter slider. Saturation is lifted so the colours are purer than the photograph, hue shifts by up to ±0.045 of the colour wheel, and lightness by ±0.1. Up to 7% of the dots (at full jitter) take the opposite hue at lower saturation, the flecks of complement that make a shadow vibrate in the divisionist manner. Because dots overlap at random, a few spots of ground show through, and the chance of that is a Poisson one.

equations.note: Number of dots for coverage slider c (0 to 1) and nominal radius r.
Chance that a pixel is under no dot at all (the 0.96 allows for the spread of dot sizes).
The jitter in hue, saturation and lightness; v is the colour jitter slider and u₁, u₂ are random numbers in [0, 1].

presets.text: Tiny dots with full coverage are close to a photograph.
Big dots with strong jitter look like a classic divisionist canvas.
A dark canvas makes the colours glow.
